title: Finn, the Giant, and the Minster of Lund
summary: A giant named Finn builds Lund Cathedral in exchange for Saint Lawrence's eyes, but the saint overhears Finn's name in a lullaby and Finn turns to stone in the crypt. This world-famous master-builder legend is connected to several European cathedrals; Finn's petrified form can still be seen grasping a pillar in the crypt of Lund Cathedral.
full_text:
In the days when Lund was still a young city, the bishop resolved to raise a minster so great that all of Skane would marvel at it. But no human builder could match the vision, and the work dragged on for years. Then Finn the giant came forward, a creature of immense stature with shoulders broad as a barn door. He offered to finish the minster in a single night, on one condition: the bishop must give him the eyes of Saint Lawrence.

The bishop agreed, though he meant to trick the giant. Finn set to work as the sun dipped below the horizon. He hauled pillars of granite as though they were fenceposts, set arches in place with a single push, and laid tiles faster than a man could count them. The sound of his hammering echoed across the flat plains, and farmers for miles around crossed themselves.

But the bishop had given a secret command: no one in the cathedral was to speak Finn's name. If the giant heard his own name before dawn, the bargain would be broken. The work went well until a nurse in the bishop's household sang a lullaby: "Hush, little one, and sleep, for Finn the giant builds the minster." Her voice carried through the still night, through the open window, and into Finn's great ear.

He froze. A roar of fury shook the vaults, and Finn seized a pillar to tear the roof apart. But the word had been spoken, and the spell was upon him. His feet rooted to the flagstones, his skin greyed and hardened, and his great arms turned to cold and ancient stone. There he stands to this day in the crypt of Lund Cathedral — a giant turned to rock, his fingers clutching a pillar, his face twisted in a snarl of thwarted rage.
moral: Knowledge is power; a name held in secret can overcome even the strongest foe.
source: The Swedish Fairy Book, ed. Clara Stroebe (1921), Ch.III: Finn, the Giant, and the Minster of Lund. Retold by Dr. v. Sydow-Lund from variants in his collection. Connected to the world-famous giant master-builder legend, also associated with Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim.

title: The Specter in Fjelkinge
summary: An innocent man is wrongly executed, and his ghost appears to the true murderer night after night until justice is done and his soul can finally rest. The tale is founded on the ancient belief that innocent blood calls for atonement.
full_text:
In the village of Fjelkinge, in the province of Skane, there lived a man known for his honesty. He was a farmer, plain and hardworking, with a wife and three children and not an enemy in the world. But envy grows in dark soil, and a neighbor who coveted his land conspired with a corrupt bailiff to accuse the farmer of theft. The evidence was fabricated, the witnesses bribed, and the farmer was condemned.

He pleaded his innocence at the gallows. "I have not stolen. God knows my heart." The rope tightened, and he was dead.

That night the true murderer could not sleep. The shadows in the corner of his room began to move, and a shape emerged — pale, translucent, with the farmer's face and steady eyes. It did not speak. It simply stood there, watching, its gaze heavy as a millstone. He screamed and lit every candle, but the specter did not leave.

Night after night it came. It followed him to the field, to the church, to the marketplace. Others began to see it too — a pale figure walking the roads in the grey hours before dawn. The guilty man grew thin and wild-eyed. He confessed at last, and the corrupt bailiff was arrested. The farmer's name was cleared.

But the specter did not leave. It walked seven more nights, slower now. On the eighth night it appeared at the farmer's grave, knelt, and pressed its pale hands to the earth. Then it rose, and a light surrounded it — warm, golden, like morning — and it was gone. The ground where it knelt grew green before all the rest, and the grass there is still greener today. Innocent blood calls for atonement, and justice, though slow, is never forgotten.
moral: Innocent blood cries out for justice, and no guilty party can escape its call.
source: The Swedish Fairy Book, ed. Clara Stroebe (1921), Ch.XXV: The Specter in Fjelkinge. Source: Hofberg, p.21. Founded on the ancient belief that innocent blood calls for atonement, and the murdered cannot rest until the deed is brought to light.
